guide.title: Canarsie, Brooklyn: The Pier Where Golden City Burned
guide.intro: Canarsie takes its name from the Canarsee, a Lenape group who lived in the area. Steam trains reached the shore in 1865, when the Brooklyn and Rockaway Beach Railroad connected Canarsie to a ferry running on to the Rockaways, and for a generation this was a waterfront day trip for the rest of Brooklyn, with hotels to match. The Golden City Amusement Park opened in 1907 on the site of today's Canarsie Pier, an attempt at a Coney Island of one's own; it burned on January 29, 1934. Typhoid outbreaks traced to Jamaica Bay shellfish in 1904 and 1915 had already ended the fishing and oystering that underpinned the local economy. Subway service arrived on July 14, 1928, the eastern marshes were filled in the 1950s for Seaview Village, the Breukelen Houses and the Bay View Houses, and the resort became a dense residential neighborhood.

sections.heading: Resort, then neighborhood
sections.body:
Canarsie's first economy was the water. Fishing and oystering supported the place until typhoid outbreaks linked to Jamaica Bay shellfish in 1904 and 1915 killed the trade. The excursion business went the same way: Golden City Amusement Park, opened in 1907 where Canarsie Pier now stands, closed with the industry's decline and burned on January 29, 1934.

What replaced it was housing. The BMT Canarsie Line began running on July 14, 1928, and in the 1950s the marshland across eastern Canarsie was filled and built on, with Seaview Village, the Breukelen Houses and the Bay View Houses going up in quick succession.

In 1972 the neighborhood became a national case study. After the local school board was ordered to accept Black students bussed in from Brownsville, Canarsie parents began protesting on October 17 and an organized school boycott ran from October 26 to November 10; of 10,000 students enrolled, only 850 attended on the first boycott day. The sociologist Jonathan Rieder documented the episode in his 1985 book "Canarsie: The Jews and Italians of Brooklyn Against Liberalism." The neighborhood that was predominantly Jewish and Italian through the 1970s is now majority Black and Caribbean.

One consequence of Canarsie's late build-out is that it carries no official landmarks at all: a 2026 survey of the neighborhood found precisely zero locations cited by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission. Its oldest buildings stand on their own merits. Grace Methodist Church, founded in 1839 as the first church in Canarsie, was the tallest building here until Holy Family's campanile went up in 1950-1951.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The L is the neighborhood's line. Canarsie–Rockaway Parkway, at Rockaway Parkway and Glenwood Road, is the L's southern terminal and sits in Canarsie; East 105th Street, between Foster Avenue and Farragut Road, is the stop before it.

From the terminal, the B42 runs along Rockaway Parkway directly down to Canarsie Pier. It began as a trolley through-service to the subway and remains the direct local link between the two.

There is no Long Island Rail Road station in or serving Canarsie, and no NYC Ferry route lists a Canarsie landing.

faq.question: How do I get to Canarsie?
faq.answer: Take the L to its southern terminal, Canarsie–Rockaway Parkway, at Rockaway Parkway and Glenwood Road, or to East 105th Street between Foster Avenue and Farragut Road. From the terminal the B42 runs down Rockaway Parkway to Canarsie Pier. There is no Long Island Rail Road station serving Canarsie and no NYC Ferry landing here.

faq.question: What was Golden City?
faq.answer: An amusement park that opened in 1907 on the site of today's Canarsie Pier, built as an answer to Coney Island. It closed as the excursion industry declined and burned down on January 29, 1934.

faq.question: Are there any landmarks in Canarsie?
faq.answer: Not officially. A 2026 survey of the neighborhood found that Canarsie has precisely zero locations cited by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission. Its historic buildings, including Grace Methodist Church of 1839 and Holy Family Roman Catholic Church of 1950-1951, carry no designation.

faq.question: What is Canarsie Pier?
faq.answer: A public pier and waterfront recreation area on Jamaica Bay at the end of Rockaway Parkway, part of the Jamaica Bay Unit of Gateway National Recreation Area and run by the National Park Service. It is used for fishing, which needs no permit during regular hours, and for waterfront walks and picnicking, and it has a restaurant and visitor facilities.

faq.question: Are there hotels in Canarsie?
faq.answer: No. Canarsie's resort era supported several hotels near the shore in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but none survive, and no lodging currently operating inside the neighborhood was found in any source consulted, including a tourism-board listing of places to stay.

places.name: Canarsie Park (Seaview Park)
places.address: Belt Parkway and Seaview Avenue, between Paerdegat Basin, East 93rd Street, East 102nd Street and Fresh Creek Basin, Brooklyn, NY 11236
places.summary: A roughly 132-acre NYC Parks property with baseball fields, a cricket field, basketball and tennis courts, a skate park, a dog run, playgrounds and a nature trail. A Parks Department historical sign on site recounts the land's Canarsee and Dutch colonial history, including Jan Martense Schenck's purchase of the surrounding land in 1675.

places.name: Canarsie Pier
places.address: End of Rockaway Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11236, extending into Jamaica Bay
places.summary: A public pier and waterfront recreation area on Jamaica Bay, part of the Jamaica Bay Unit of Gateway National Recreation Area and operated by the National Park Service. It is used for fishing, which requires no permit during regular hours, and for waterfront walks and picnicking, and it has a restaurant and visitor-facing facilities.
places.history: The site was a Canarsee canoe-launching point, and later the location of the Golden City Amusement Park, which opened in 1907 and burned on January 29, 1934.

places.name: Brooklyn Terminal Market
places.address: Adjacent to Canarsie Plaza on Avenue D, Brooklyn, NY 11236
places.summary: A wholesale and retail horticultural market selling plants, trees and fruit, next to the Canarsie Plaza shopping center on Avenue D.

places.name: Grace Methodist Church (Church at the Rock)
places.address: East 92nd Street, south of Avenue J, Canarsie, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: Founded in 1839 as the first church in Canarsie, and now Church at the Rock. The present gambrel-roofed building was dedicated in 1895, incorporating an earlier structure of 1871, and it was the tallest building in Canarsie until Holy Family's campanile surpassed it. Like every site in the neighborhood, it carries no city landmark designation.

places.name: Holy Family Roman Catholic Church
places.address: Rockaway Parkway and Flatlands Avenue, Canarsie, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: Built in 1950-1951, its campanile became the tallest structure in Canarsie. It is not a city-designated landmark.

places.name: Canarsie Cemetery
places.address: Remsen Avenue and Avenue K, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A city-owned cemetery with roughly 6,400 interments, among them Civil War and Spanish-American War veterans.
places.history: The Remsen family owned the ground until 1888, when it passed to the Town of Flatlands. It became New York City property with the consolidation of 1898.

places.name: Armando's Pizza
places.summary: A neighborhood pizzeria on Rockaway Parkway, described as a Canarsie staple operating since 1960.

places.name: TriniJam BK Roti Bar & Grill
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant blending Trinidadian and Jamaican cooking, with curry goat, jerk chicken and roti on the menu. Restaurant Guru named it Best BBQ in New York City in 2023.

places.name: Spread Love & Eat
places.summary: A local eat-and-drink spot on Flatlands Avenue.
